global_facts.detail: Danish Health Data Authority states 17 countries had at least one MyHealth@EU service in routine operation at the start of January 2026.
global_facts.quote: At the beginning of January 2026, 17 countries had one or more solutions in routine operations, exchanging health data across borders with one or more other countries.

global_facts.detail: EHDS applies in general from 26 March 2027. Patient summaries, ePrescriptions and eDispensations fall under the 2029 date; images, test results and discharge reports under the 2031 date.
global_facts.publisher: EUR-Lex, Official Journal of the European Union (text read via the Publications Office Cellar)
global_facts.quote: This Regulation shall apply from 26 March 2027.

global_facts.detail: Rights and cross-border exchange (Articles 3 to 15, 23(2) to (6)) apply to patient summaries, ePrescriptions and eDispensations from 26 March 2029.
global_facts.publisher: EUR-Lex, Official Journal of the European Union (text read via the Publications Office Cellar)
global_facts.quote: from 26 March 2029 to priority categories of personal electronic health data referred to in Article 14(1), points (a), (b) and (c)

global_facts.detail: The same provisions apply to medical images, test results and discharge reports from 26 March 2031.
global_facts.publisher: EUR-Lex, Official Journal of the European Union (text read via the Publications Office Cellar)
global_facts.quote: from 26 March 2031 to priority categories of personal electronic health data referred to in Article 14(1), points (d), (e) and (f)

global_facts.detail: Article 14(1) defines the six priority categories in order: (a) patient summaries, (b) electronic prescriptions, (c) electronic dispensations, (d) imaging, (e) test results, (f) discharge reports.
global_facts.publisher: EUR-Lex, Official Journal of the European Union (text read via the Publications Office Cellar)
global_facts.quote: medical imaging studies and related imaging reports;

global_facts.detail: Under EHDS a person may download a free electronic copy of the priority data in the European exchange format. For EU countries this is the person-carried fallback from 26 March 2029 (summaries and prescriptions) and 2031 (other categories).
global_facts.publisher: EUR-Lex, Official Journal of the European Union (text read via the Publications Office Cellar)
global_facts.quote: shall have the right to download free of charge an electronic copy of at least the personal electronic health data in the priority categories referred to in Article 14

global_facts.detail: Every Member State must connect its national contact point to MyHealth@EU and exchange the priority categories, on the application dates above.
global_facts.publisher: EUR-Lex, Official Journal of the European Union (text read via the Publications Office Cellar)
global_facts.quote: Each national contact point for digital health shall enable the exchange of the personal electronic health data referred to in Article 14(1) with national contact points for digital health in other Member States through MyHealth@EU.

global_facts.detail: A non-EU country can join MyHealth@EU only as an authorised participant after Commission compliance checks and an implementing act. The Commission must keep a public list of connected third countries.
global_facts.publisher: EUR-Lex, Official Journal of the European Union (text read via the Publications Office Cellar)
global_facts.quote: A national contact point for digital health of a third country or a system established at international level by an international organisation may become an authorised participant in MyHealth@EU

global_facts.detail: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2083 of 18 September 2026 sets the rules for MyHealth@EU under EHDS and applies from 26 March 2027. It lists no participating countries.
global_facts.publisher: EUR-Lex, Official Journal of the European Union (text read via the Publications Office Cellar)

global_facts.detail: The regulation confirms the current infrastructure is voluntary: countries exchange patient summaries, ePrescriptions and eDispensations by choice until EHDS obligations apply.
global_facts.publisher: EUR-Lex, Official Journal of the European Union (text read via the Publications Office Cellar)
global_facts.quote: That infrastructure allowed Member States to exchange patient summaries, electronic prescriptions and electronic dispensations on a voluntary basis.

global_facts.detail: Contact points already exchanging data before 26 March 2029 may continue under the new rules without a new authorisation.
global_facts.publisher: EUR-Lex, Official Journal of the European Union (text read via the Publications Office Cellar)
global_facts.quote: may continue to exchange such data in the framework of MyHealth@EU and shall be deemed to comply with the authorisation requirements

global_facts.detail: The Commission page describes the two services as being introduced, open to all EU countries, and points to the KPI maps for which services run where. Its country list covers EU members plus Iceland and Norway.
global_facts.quote: The exchange of ePrescriptions and Patient Summaries is open to all the EU countries.

global_facts.detail: The Commission page describes the scope as travel within the EU.
global_facts.quote: The eHealth Digital Service Infrastructure (eHDSI) is an infrastructure ensuring the continuity of care for European citizens while they are travelling abroad in the EU.

global_facts.detail: Commission snapshot written in early 2025 (not current): 13 countries live with at least one service, a 2025 cohort and Slovakia in 2026. Treat as history, not as status on 2 Oct 2026.
global_facts.quote: Czech Republic, Estonia, Greece, Finland, France, Croatia, Ireland, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Latvia, Malta, Poland and Portugal are live with at least one service. In 2025 Austria, Cyprus, Denmark, Hungary, Island, Italy, Norway, Romania, Sweden and Slovenia will join and Slovakia in 2026.

global_facts.detail: Same page: 15 Member States supported the services at the time of writing.
global_facts.quote: Today, 15 EU Member States support sharing patient summaries and ePrescriptions via MyHealth@EU.

global_facts.detail: The KPI site itself warns that the published figures are being revised. The transaction layers end on 30 June 2025.

refs.text: Only private clinics have a written duty to give patients a copy of their clinical records, under a 2012 regulation. There is no national patient portal, and records are still mostly on paper.

Article 34 of the Private Health Centres Regulation (Official Gazette No. 1084, August 2012) says the head of a private health centre must give the patient a copy of the clinical records, including examination and treatment reports, after treatment ends. The centre keeps another copy for 10 years.
We found no matching rule for state hospitals and clinics. The Public Health Law sets a duty of medical secrecy, but we found no clause giving patients a right to see or copy their record.
There is no patient portal. A 2026 study quotes a ministry staff member: "Our system is still mostly paper-based." We found no national or hospital patient portal in ministry sources.

refs.text: Article 26 of the 2011 data law gives a free right to learn what data is held, but health data is seen only through a doctor the patient chooses. There is no fixed deadline and no national patient portal.
The 1992 health basis law (Lei 21-B/92, art. 13) gives users a right to be informed about their condition and treatment options. It does not set a right to a copy of the clinical file.
We found no national or provider patient portal. Score: base 45, minus 5 for no deadline, minus 5 for the doctor-only route.

refs.text: The 2024 data protection law gives a free right of access within 30 days, but no national portal shows the medical record. Only pieces are online, such as a person's own e-prescriptions on e-Albania, so the score sits at 50.

Article 14 of Law 124/2024 lets a person get confirmation and access to their personal data from any controller within 30 days. Article 12 makes the answer free, and Article 14 allows a reasonable fee only for later copies.
The 2009 Health Care Law (Article 30) says health documentation may stay with the institution or be owned by the patient, but sets no specific right to a copy of the record.

The government portal e-Albania offers "Receta ime elektronike", a view of a person's own electronic prescriptions. How many people it covers, and whether e-Albania shows other parts of the medical record, was not verified.
In June 2026 opposition MPs said public hospitals still lack an electronic medical record. A national patient portal with a full record was not found.

refs.text: Llei 20/2017 gives a right to the whole record, with copies within five working days. The national Andorra Salut app shows reports, test results and vaccinations, but it needs a digital certificate and has about 25,000 users.

Article 43 of Llei 20/2017 gives the patient access to the clinical record and all the documents in it. The patient must be informed of its content within five working days at most, and copies are delivered in the same period.

The Andorra Salut app, created in 2021, shows medical reports, test results, vaccination records and appointments (WHO Observatory, 2026). A February 2026 update added pending referrals and tests, and a QR code to share results with doctors outside Andorra.

The government reported over 50,000 downloads, 25,000 users and about 5,000 connections a month. Access requires a digital certificate. We did not verify an official figure on the share of residents who use it, or a machine-readable export.

refs.text: No federal law gives patients a right to a copy of their record; the right sits in Abu Dhabi and Dubai regulator standards. Three government portals show part of the record by region, which lifts the cell to the top of its band (35) and no further.

Federal Law No. 2 of 2019 on ICT in health sets confidentiality, a central exchange and 25-year retention, but none of its 31 articles gives the patient a right to see or copy the record. The general privacy law, Decree-Law 45 of 2021, does not apply to health data that has its own law (Article 2).

Abu Dhabi's 2020 DOH privacy standard says that, except in certain circumstances, patients have the right to review and obtain a copy of their records. Dubai's 2022 DHA policy grants a subject access request for a copy, answered within one month. No federal equivalent for the Northern Emirates was opened.

Abu Dhabi residents see Malaffi data in the Sahatna app: lab and microbiology results, radiology reports, visits and e-prescriptions, but only from Abu Dhabi facilities connected to Malaffi. MOHAP's Smart Patient Portal shows lab tests, radiology reports, documents, medicines, vaccinations and allergies.

Dubai's DHA app shows appointment history, lab results and medications. Whether it shows records from private facilities through NABIDH was not verified. No portal offers machine-readable export, and no official figure on portal use was found.

refs.text: The law gives patients a right to see and copy their medical files, and the ArMed portal shows diagnoses, services and tests entered by clinics. How complete the portal is for privately paid care was not verified.
Article 14 of the 1996 Law on Medical Assistance gives every patient the right to see their medical files, including electronic ones, or get copies under the Freedom of Information Law procedure.

Article 8 of the medical law gives each patient an electronic access window in the e-health system. The ArMed operator says 2.9 million citizens have a personal medical card, opened with an ID card PIN or the app.

The operator says the portal shows diagnoses, services, and lab and instrumental tests as entered by clinics. An undated operator page says only state-funded visits were shown at that stage, so current coverage is not verified. Score sits in the lower half of the 60 to 75 band.

refs.text: The Data Protection Act 2013 gives a right to a copy within 30 days, for a prescribed fee, but defines personal data around commercial transactions. There is no patient portal, so access means a written request to each provider.

Sections 12 to 15 of the Data Protection Act 2013 require a public or private body, on a written request and the prescribed fee, to answer within 30 days and let the person examine or copy their data. The deadline can be extended by up to 30 more days.
The Medical Council Code of Ethics says providers own records but patients have a right of access. No patient portal, national or hospital, was found.

refs.text: Patients have a statutory right to see their records and get a free first copy, and the ELGA portal shows discharge letters, lab and radiology reports and 18 months of medicines. Images, GP notes and documents from before 2016 are missing, and uptake is low.

Section 51 of the Medical Practitioners Act obliges doctors to let patients inspect their records and to give a first copy free. The federal hospitals act (KAKuG § 10) makes hospitals grant inspection and copies under GDPR Article 15(3).

With ID Austria, patients can view, download and print ELGA documents: discharge letters, lab and radiology reports, outpatient reports and the e-medication list. Medication data are deleted after 18 months, and hospital documents are only there from 2016.

The official portal does not show images. Die Presse reported in February 2026 that one hospital group's app was the first to display X-ray and MRI images; ELGA GmbH says portal viewing and download are still planned.

No official figure on portal use was found. The Kronen Zeitung reported in May 2025 that fewer than 100,000 people use ELGA. People without ID Austria can view records at regional ELGA ombudsman offices.

refs.text: The law gives a free first copy, paper or electronic, within 15 days, and the EU rates Belgian record access 100 out of 100. The federal portal shows linked documents, not one full record, and French speakers cannot see vaccines or test results in the app.

Article 9 of the law of 22 August 2002 gives the right to consult the file within 15 days of a request and to receive explanations. The first copy is free, the patient chooses paper or electronic, and later copies may cost only reasonable, justified fees.

The federal Masanté portal and app show open prescriptions, vaccinations, a health summary, screening results, medical reports and results, and up to one year of dispensed medicines, on the web and in a mobile app (INAMI).

refs.text: The Civil Code lets patients read and copy listed record types, and the 2013 rules list what hospitals may copy, leaving out progress notes, with a fee and no fixed deadline. Public health files are opening to residents county by county, a target for 2026.

Civil Code Article 1225 says hospitals must 'promptly' provide admission notes, orders, test reports, operation and anaesthesia records, pathology and nursing records when a patient asks to read or copy them. PIPL Article 45 adds a general right to read and copy personal information.

The 2013 Medical Record Management Rules (Article 19) list what a hospital may copy, from temperature charts to imaging. Progress notes and case discussions are not on the list. Copies are made with the patient present and may carry a cost fee (Article 23).
Records are kept at least 15 years for outpatients and 30 years for inpatients (Article 29). There is no national portal for hospital charts.

Score follows the statutory-right rule: base 45, minus 5 each for the fee, no fixed deadline and limited scope, plus 5 because the official 2026 notice documents a resident health file portal. No wide-use figure was found, so no further credit.

refs.text: Law 29-2019 lets a patient ask for their health data, directly or through a doctor they choose, and get a copy. The provider may charge the cost of copying, no deadline is set, and there is no patient portal, so 35.

Article 50 of Law 29-2019 lets any person who proves their identity ask a controller, in writing, whether it holds their data, for what purpose, and for a copy in accessible form. Article 51 says a copy must be given on request.
Article 51 lets the controller charge up to the cost of reproduction. We found no deadline for answering an access request. The one-month deadline in Article 60 covers corrections, not copies.

Portability to another provider (Article 56) covers only consent-based automated processing and excludes public-interest tasks. The 2023-2026 health plan describes data collected mostly on paper, and we found no national portal or app showing patients their records.

refs.text: The 2025 Digital Code gives a right to a copy within one month, directly or through a chosen doctor, but copies can cost the reproduction price. Public bodies, which run most care, have two years to comply and there is no portal, so 35.
Articles 32 and 33 of the Digital Code (Law 019/AN/23, published 18 September 2025) give a right to know what data is held and to get a copy. A request made electronically gets an electronic answer.
Article 25 sets a one-month deadline, extendable by two months. Article 22 makes rights free in general, but Article 33 lets the controller charge up to the cost of reproduction for a copy.

Article 34 says health data can be accessed by the person directly or through a doctor of their choice. Article 46 adds portability in a machine-readable format for data processed by consent or contract.

Public bodies have two years from entry into force to comply (Article 784). A January 2026 fact sheet said it was unclear whether a data authority had been appointed, and we found no decree naming its members. We found no national portal where patients can see their record.

refs.text: Law 025/2023 gives a free written right to see your data and a copy, directly or through a doctor. No deadline is set, the provider may charge the cost of copying, and there is no patient portal, so 35.

Article 43 of Law 025/2023 lets any person who proves their identity ask a controller, free of charge and in writing, for their data in an accessible form and its source. A request made electronically is answered in a common electronic format. A copy is provided; reasonable fees apply only to extra copies.

Article 44 contradicts this in part: it lets the controller make the copy depend on a payment no higher than the cost of reproduction. We found no deadline for answering an access request in Articles 43 to 49.

Electronic patient files exist in some pilot hospitals under the eGabon-SIS project, but they are tools for staff. We found no national portal or app that shows patients their own record. The CNAMGS insurance eServices portal handles insured-person services, and we could not see what it shows behind its login.

Article 17 of the 2000 Law on Patient Rights lets patients see their medical records, ask for corrections and request a copy of any part. The request goes in writing to the medical facility.
Article 14 of the 2023 Personal Data Protection Law gives a free copy within 10 working days, extendable by 10. Controllers may charge a reasonable fee for other formats or frequent requests.

The EHR order (consolidated text as of 18 February 2026) gives a patient page showing the patient's episodes and processing logs. The State Audit Office says that page did not work during its audit and opened only in November 2024. How the live portal works today is not verified.

The auditor found 89 of 150 surveyed patients had not heard of the EHR, and 50% of 2022-2023 state-programme cases were not recorded. No official usage figure was found, so the score follows the statutory-right formula: base 45, +5 free with deadline, +5 official portal.

refs.text: Kurdistan's Law No. 4 of 2020 gives patients a free copy of their medical file, but we found no matching federal right for the rest of Iraq. The insurer's Damani platform holds an electronic file, but the patient features described are booking, covered services and remaining visits.

Article 3 of the Kurdistan Region's Law No. 4 of 2020 gives every patient, in public or private care, the right to see their medical file and get a copy on request, and a medical report, without charge.

The Kurdistan health ministry's Instruction No. 4 of 2022 adds a right to request a medical report and copies of test results. It restates the right to see and copy the record in its section on patients with AIDS.
For federal Iraq we found no law giving patients a right to see or copy their record. A federal right was not verified, so the score stays in the band for rights that cover only some people.

The Health Insurance Fund says its Damani app lets members register, add family, see covered services and track how many yearly visits remain. Whether patients can open their own medical file in the app was not verified.

refs.text: The Patient's Rights Act gives a right to the record and a copy, and a 2019 ministry circular makes all four health funds show members structured and free-text data online. No fixed deadline was found and no official usage figure was verified.

Section 18(a) of the Patient's Rights Act 1996 entitles a patient to medical information from their record, including a copy. A clinician may withhold information that could cause serious harm, but must refer the decision to the ethics committee, which can reverse it.

The 2019 fee regulations make online viewing free and cap a computerised copy at NIS 10 per request, for records created in the five years before the request. Discharge letters, test results and follow-up instructions are free once per episode. No statutory deadline for answering a request was found.

Circular 8/2019 requires each health fund (every resident belongs to one) to show structured and free-text record data in a personal online file, plus data from the national exchange, with print and download. Funds may keep clinicians' internal note fields hidden. Clalit's app lists diagnoses, tests, sensitivities, medicines and vaccines.

Full copies are still requested institution by institution, since the fee rules treat each hospital or health fund record as a unit. The share of residents who use the portals was not verified. The 2024 Portability Law will add a right to move data between providers, but it starts on 24 July 2027.

Section 26 of the Data Protection Act 2019 gives a right of access, and section 38 a right to a machine-readable copy. Regulation 9 of the 2021 General Regulations says a controller must answer within seven days, free of charge, and in electronic form when asked electronically.

Regulation 18 of the 2025 health information rules says patients may see and share their Shared Health Record through the patient portal.

The Afyangu app shows 500,000+ downloads on Google Play. A December 2025 feature said three million Kenyans use the platform; that figure is not verified by an official source. Scored as statutory right plus free, fixed deadline plus an officially documented portal (45 + 5 + 5).

refs.text: Dutch law gives a copy of the whole file and free electronic access, and about 93% of GPs connect to certified apps. Only 571,000 people fetched records that way in 2024, and the EU scores Dutch record access 69.35 against an 86.51 average.

Article 7:456 of the Civil Code (WGBO) gives the patient access to and a copy of the data in the file, limited only to protect another person's privacy. The provider must keep the file for 20 years after the last change (art. 7:454).

Article 15d of the Wabvpz requires providers to give access and copies electronically on request, free of charge. Pharmacists must show medication data electronically on request, at dispensing. GDPR one-month deadlines also apply.

There is no government portal. Patients use apps with the MedMij label (PGOs). MedMij says 4,388 providers exchanged data with these apps in December 2024, including 93% of GPs and 83% of medical specialist institutions. Users fetched records 1.6 million times in 2024.

MedMij is a national label for private apps, not a government portal, so the no-portal rule applies: base 45, +5 free copy with a fixed deadline, +5 apps documented officially. No +10: 93% of GPs are connected, but 571,000 users in 2024 is not wide use.

refs.text: Norway has a statutory right to see and copy the whole record, and Helsenorge logged 104.7 million logins in 2025. But GP records are not on Helsenorge, and the Commission found imaging reports and images are not online at all.

Section 5-1 of the Patient and User Rights Act gives a right to see the record and, on request, a copy (GDPR Article 15). Refusal is allowed only to prevent danger to life or serious harm, or where access is clearly inadvisable for people close to the patient. GDPR adds a one month deadline and a free first copy.

Helsenorge's Pasientjournal service shows documents from selected hospitals in Helse Nord, Vest and Sør-Øst, plus Oslo's emergency services. Hospitals in Central Norway do not show records there; they use their own portal, HelsaMi. GP records are not available on Helsenorge, so patients must ask their GP for a copy.

Use is heavy. Helsedirektoratet counted 104.7 million logins in 2025, about 8.7 million a month. Patients must be 16 or older to see their hospital record online, and parents of children aged 12 to 16 must ask the hospital for a copy.

In 2024, 40% of Portuguese adults accessed their record online, against 28% in the EU, but 62% of the most educated did so versus 19% of the least educated (OECD). Since early 2026 the app also shows five years of care history (E-Konomista).

refs.text: Article 7:456 of the Civil Code, in force since 1 May 2025, gives a right to inspect and copy the medical file, with no fixed deadline and a fee allowed for copies. The My Health app shows part of the record for patients of about 63 listed GPs.

Article 456 of Book 7 says the care provider gives the patient, on request and as soon as possible, inspection of and a copy of the file. The provider may charge a reasonable fee for the copy. Information that would harm another person's privacy is held back.

The new Civil Code took effect on 1 May 2025 after the President decided against requests for delay. A doctor writing in Starnieuws in September 2026 said patients now have a direct legal right to read and copy what the doctor wrote.

The Ministry of Health launched the My Health app in May 2025. It shows medical advice, vital signs and diagnoses from certified GP record systems. Patients activate it with a QR code from their own GP.

The Ministry's list of activation sites names 63 doctors in the Paramaribo region, plus a Nickerie list of 10 that repeats names from it. No user figure was found. Under the access rules this is base 45, minus 5 for the fee and 5 for no fixed deadline, plus 5 for an officially documented portal.

refs.text: The law gives patients the right to see their whole record without delay, and the national electronic health book (EZK) is online through the National Health Portal. Login needs a chip ID card with an activated e-signature, minors cannot log in, and usage figures were not verified.

Act 576/2004, section 25, says records are made available without delay to the patient or legal representative in full, and the patient may make extracts or copies on site. Anyone refused access can go to court.

Act 153/2013, section 5(5), lets a person read their EZK through the National Health Portal with an official authenticator. NCZI says this needs an eID card with an activated electronic signature and a security code, and that minors currently cannot log in.

The EZK holds a patient summary, prescriptions and dispensing, examination records and lab results, but lab coverage is still growing. How many residents use the EZK was not verified, so the score sits in the lower half of the portal band.

refs.text: Section 27 of the Data Protection Act 2023 gives a free right to your data but sets no reply deadline, and the regulator says the Act risks going largely unenforced. There is no national patient portal, so patients ask the health service directly.

Section 27 of the Data Protection Act 2023 gives a right to confirmation, a copy of the data being processed, its origin, its recipients and the legal basis. Section 25(8) says this must be free unless a request is manifestly unfounded or excessive.

Section 31 adds a right to get data in a structured, machine-readable and interoperable format, or to move it to another controller. The Act sets no fixed deadline to answer a request. The Minister may set timelines by regulation.

The 2026 Budget describes the state electronic Health Information System (eHIS) as giving records to authorised providers and SMS appointment reminders. It mentions no patient portal, and we found none.
Score: base 45 for a statutory right with no national portal, plus 5 for a free copy in a structured format, minus 5 for no fixed deadline, minus 5 for weak enforcement (see privacy).

refs.text: Public patients can get their hospital file through a Freedom of Information Act request, decided within 30 days, but copies carry a fee. Private clinics are not covered because the data protection rules for business were never brought into force, and there is no portal.

The Freedom of Information Act 1999 covers every Regional Health Authority (RHA). Requests are free and decided within 30 days (section 15). Copies carry a prescribed fee, waived if the 30-day deadline is missed and refunded if access is not given within seven working days of payment (section 17). Section 36 lets a person ask to correct personal information.
The South West RHA tells patients to use a Freedom of Information Act request form to get a copy of their medical record. Its patient charter says patients have the right to a copy of their records.
The Data Protection Act 2011 would give an access right against private bodies too, but those parts have not been proclaimed. No patient portal for hospital records was found.
Score: base 45, minus 5 for limited scope (public bodies only), minus 5 for the per-copy fee.

us_note.detail: Under HIPAA a person has a right to inspect and get a copy of their health information held in a designated record set, and can carry it anywhere.
us_note.publisher: eCFR, 45 CFR 164.524 (US Government Publishing Office / Office of the Federal Register)
us_note.quote: an individual has a right of access to inspect and obtain a copy of protected health information about the individual in a designated record set

us_note.detail: If the record is held electronically and the person asks for an electronic copy, the provider must give it in the electronic form requested if readily producible, or an agreed readable electronic form.
us_note.quote: if the individual requests an electronic copy of such information, the covered entity must provide the individual with access to the protected health information in the electronic form and format requested by the individual, if it is readily producible in such form and format

us_note.detail: A person can direct the provider to send the copy straight to someone they name, which is how a US patient can route a record to a clinician abroad.
us_note.quote: If an individual's request for access directs the covered entity to transmit the copy of protected health information directly to another person designated by the individual, the covered entity must provide the copy to the person designated by the individual.

us_note.detail: TEFCA is a framework for sharing records within the United States; it is domestic and has no link to foreign exchanges.
us_note.publisher: Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy / ONC, HHS
us_note.quote: The Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement™, known as TEFCA®, operates in the United States as a nationwide framework for health information sharing.

us_note.detail: The 21st Century Cures Act information blocking rules bar practices that interfere with access to or exchange of electronic health information, supporting patient access through apps.
us_note.publisher: Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy / ONC, HHS
us_note.quote: Information Blocking Prevents practices that interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information, as defined by the Cures Act.

refs.text: Law 15/2023 lets patients read and copy their record on written request, and Decree 356 sets a 10-day deadline. VNeID shows visit summaries, labs and drugs as downloadable PDFs, but only 34 million people had one in September 2026, short of most residents.

Article 12 of Law 15/2023 on medical examination and treatment gives patients the right to read, view, copy and take notes on their record and to get a record summary. Article 69(4)(d) says this applies to records that are complete and archived, on a written request. The law text sets no fee and no deadline.

Under Decision 31/QĐ-BYT of January 2026, the VNeID health book shows allergies, history, vaccinations, each visit's diagnosis, test values, drugs and procedures, and a discharge summary. Patients can download each visit as a PDF. Machine-readable export was not found.

Coverage: the Ministry of Health counted 34,023,412 people with a VNeID health book on 16 September 2026 (reported by VOV, the state broadcaster). That is well short of most of Vietnam's residents, so the 60 to 75 portal band is not reached.

Score: base 45 for a statutory right with no portal reaching most residents, plus 5 for the 10-day PDP deadline, plus 10 for an official portal with an official usage figure, giving 60, the top of that ladder. The Law 15 limit to archived records is offset by the PDP right, which covers all personal data.

refs.text: Two laws give a right to a copy: the 2019 data law makes the first copy free within one month, but the patient rights law puts copies at the patient's cost. With no national portal, the free copy (+5) and the charge (-5) cancel at 45.

Article 19 of Law 2004/38 lets a resident see the data in an institution's health documentation, get copies at their own cost, receive the final report, and ask for errors to be corrected without deleting the original entry.

Law 06/L-082 (Article 14) gives a right of access and a copy of personal data. Article 11 requires a free answer within one month, extendable by two months; under Article 14 only further copies may carry an administrative fee.
No national portal showing a person's medical record was found. The World Bank says the legacy systems run in silos, and it was not verified whether any of them shows records to patients.

refs.text: Law No. 13 of 2012 lets a person see only the personal data they gave a public body, so it is not a right to the whole chart. With paper records in most facilities and no portal, Yemen sits between Sudan (22) and Iraq (30).
Public bodies must answer requests within 15 days and may charge only the actual cost of copies. Article 25 requires officials to refuse personal data whose disclosure would invade privacy.
The 2002 medical professions law makes doctors keep a register of patient visits and diagnoses (Article 11) and lets them share secrets with the patient (Article 23). It sets no right to a copy.
The World Bank found paper systems in most of 5,393 facilities in 2024. We found no patient portal. Whether the Commissioner-General's complaints office works today was not verified.

refs.text: POPIA section 23 and PAIA give a right to your record within 30 days, but providers may charge a prescribed fee and no national patient portal was found. Scored as statutory right (45) minus 5 for the fee.

The National Health Act (section 13) makes facilities keep a record for every user but does not itself spell out a patient's right to a copy. HPCSA Booklet 9 says state institutions must give copies on request for a reasonable PAIA fee, and anyone aged 12 or over may get their own records.

The Department of Health says every user should have a portable electronic record that belongs to the patient, carried on HPRS. That is a design goal tied to NHI. We found no public portal where patients read their own record.

refs.text: The Data Protection Act 2021 gives a right to a copy, which may be free for the first copy and comes in electronic format on request, but sets no deadline. We found no patient portal, so people ask each facility.

Section 58 of the Data Protection Act 2021 lets a person confirm what data is held, see its purpose and recipients, and get a copy. A controller may give the first copy at no cost; extra copies may cost a reasonable administrative fee. Electronic requests get a commonly used electronic format.

The Health Professions Council's 2016 records guideline says health records are the property of the facility, but practitioners must give patients a copy, abstract or direct access on request. It allows a reasonable fee for copies, which predates the 2021 Act.
We found no national patient portal or app for viewing the SmartCare record. Access works provider by provider.

refs.text: Section 14 of the Cyber and Data Protection Act 2021 gives a right to access personal information, but sets no deadline or format. No patient portal was verified, so patients ask each provider.

The Cyber and Data Protection Act 2021 gives every data subject a right to access personal information held by a controller, and rights to object, correct and delete false data. The Act text we read sets no deadline, fee rule or machine-readable format for that request.

The Medical Services Amendment Act 2026 adds duties to tell patients their health status and treatment options, and to give a discharge report on leaving hospital. It does not create a right to a full copy of the record.

The national Impilo record is a clinician system. No patient-facing portal showing a person's own record was verified. Score follows the anchor: statutory right, no national portal, minus 5 for no fixed deadline.
